transcript.text:
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for being here. As you all know, the Department of Justice has issued a subpoena concerning commission payments made through our international distributors, and we need to provide an initial response and proposed investigation plan next month. Our current response packet describes the matter as an inquiry into distributor commissions, but it does not yet specify whether we will make a voluntary disclosure, a repayment amount, or an executive-interview protocol.

Before we can finalize anything, I need each of you — white-collar, finance, and employment counsel — to give me your final recommendation on every open response item. Once I've heard from all three of you, I'll record a definitive yes-or-no decision on voluntary disclosure and the other terms, along with implementation commitments. That's non-negotiable — this meeting doesn't end until those decisions are on the record.

So let's start with the basics. White-collar counsel, can you walk us through your recommendation on voluntary disclosure? Finance, I'll need your assessment of any repayment exposure. And employment counsel, I'll need your guidance on the executive-interview protocol. Let's get into it.

transcript.text:
Thank you, Elena. Let me put my recommendation on the record.

On voluntary disclosure: Given that we have a confirmed DOJ subpoena, a clearly defined scope of four distributors across calendar years 2019 through 2021, and — as Maya has just confirmed — a quantified $275,000 in improper payments that controllership has already reconciled, my recommendation is yes, we should make a voluntary disclosure. The scope is now sufficiently defined for us to do so meaningfully, and voluntary disclosure positions us far better in any subsequent negotiation or resolution with the government than waiting for them to extract the information through enforcement. It also demonstrates good-faith cooperation, which can materially affect charging and sentencing outcomes.

I would add one condition to that recommendation: my subpoena-scope memorandum is still in review, and I want it finalized and incorporated into the response packet before we submit, so that our disclosure accurately reflects the four-distributor, 2019–2021 parameters. I don't want us to over-disclose beyond what the subpoena actually covers, nor under-disclose within that scope.

So, to be clear: my final recommendation on voluntary disclosure is yes, subject to completing the scope memorandum review and updating the response packet accordingly before submission.

I'll defer to Maya on the repayment amount and to Jordan on the executive-interview protocol, as those are within their respective lanes. But from the white-collar perspective, I support moving forward promptly on disclosure given what we now know.

transcript.text:
Thank you, Elena. Let me put my recommendation on the record.

On the repayment amount: Given that I have completed a reconciliation of the commission ledger and supporting invoices showing exactly $275,000 in improper payments — confirmed with controllership just yesterday — my recommendation is that we propose a repayment of $275,000 to the government as part of our response packet. This figure is now well-documented and backed by invoice-level evidence, so we have a defensible, quantified basis for the repayment rather than an estimate.

I would add two conditions to that recommendation. First, before we submit, the $275,000 figure and the underlying reconciliation need to be formally incorporated into the investigation materials — right now it has not been added, and I don't want us citing a number in our response that isn't supported in the workpapers. Second, I want controllership to provide a written sign-off on the reconciliation so that our repayment proposal rests on documented finance verification, not just my working file.

So, to be clear: my final recommendation on the repayment amount is $275,000, subject to (1) incorporating the reconciliation into the investigation materials and (2) obtaining controllership's written sign-off before submission.

I'll defer to Jordan on the executive-interview protocol, but from a finance perspective, the $275,000 is the number I'm comfortable putting forward.

transcript.text:
Thank you, Elena. Let me put my recommendation on the record.

On the executive-interview protocol: Given that the implicated vice president has retained separate counsel and will not participate in a company interview without that counsel's written consent, my recommendation is that we do not attempt to compel or schedule an interview with the VP at this stage. Forcing the issue without separate counsel's written sign-off creates significant employment-law risk — potential claims of coercion, interference with the employee's right to counsel, and exposure under our policies on employee representation in internal investigations. The prudent path is to work through the VP's counsel to establish a mutually agreeable interview framework, including scope, timing, and any limitations, before proceeding.

I would add two conditions to that recommendation. First, I am still waiting for the engagement letter from the VP's counsel to be filed — once it is, I will circulate the written confirmation so that everyone has a clear record of the representation and its parameters. Second, I want the interview protocol to be documented in writing and agreed to by the VP's counsel before any interview takes place, so that we have a clear understanding of what topics are covered, whether the interview will be under oath or recorded, and what access the company will have to any notes or statements.

So, to be clear: my final recommendation on the executive-interview protocol is that we do not proceed with the VP interview without separate counsel's written consent, that we negotiate the interview terms through the VP's counsel, and that we wait for the engagement letter to be filed before formalizing any protocol. We can proceed with other investigative steps in the meantime — document collection, custodian interviews, and the scope and reconciliation work Thomas and Maya have described — but the VP interview specifically should not be on the calendar until these conditions are met.
